body.text: Canadian businesses exploring incentives such as the tax credit for apprentices should also understand the SR&ED program: under the Income Tax Act, corporations, individuals and partnership members performing qualifying research in Canada can claim a 15% to 35% investment tax credit on qualified SR&ED salaries and expenditures, with qualifying CCPCs earning up to $2.1 million in refundable credits annually.

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is the federal government's cornerstone fiscal mechanism for subsidizing industrial innovation, delivering $4.6 billion in allowed Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) across 24,160 corporate and individual claims in fiscal year 2025/26. Governed jointly by Section 37, Section 127, Section 127.1, and Subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) alongside Part XXIX (Sections 2900 to 2903) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945), the program provides two distinct, interlocking statutory incentives: (1) an immediate or indefinitely carryforwardable deduction against business income via the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, and (2) an Investment Tax Credit ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, Canada enacted the most expansive structural overhaul of the SR&ED regime since the March 29, 2012 federal budget. Initiated in the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement (which initially proposed raising the enhanced expenditure limit from $3.0 million to $4.5 million), expanded in the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget tabled by Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne, and enacted into law via Bill C-15 (which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026), these reforms apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. First, the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC was doubled from $3.0 million to $6.0 million, increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund on current expenditures from $1.05 million to $2.1 million. Second, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) were widened from the legacy $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million. Third, eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC was extended for the first time to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), subject to a $15 million–$75 million phase-out based on three-year consolidated average annual gross revenue—a calculation method that CCPCs may also elect to use under Subsection 127(10.32). Fourth, the eligibility of capital expenditures (depreciable property used all or substantially all in SR&ED, equipment lease costs, and first- and second-term Shared-Use Equipment [SUE])—which had been repealed since January 1, 2014—was formally restored for property acquired and available for use, or lease amounts first becoming payable, after December 15, 2024.

At the sub-national level, provincial alignment with the post-December 15, 2024 federal reforms has diverged sharply, requiring granular multi-jurisdictional tax modelling. British Columbia expressly harmonized its SR&ED tax credit with the federal expansion, raising its refundable expenditure cap from $3.0 million to $6.0 million, adopting the $15 million–$75 million taxable capital phase-out, extending refundability to ECPCs, restoring capital expenditure eligibility, and making its provincial credit permanent in B.C. Budget 2026. Conversely, Quebec fundamentally restructured its provincial innovation architecture for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing up to eight legacy R&D tax measures with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation—CRIC), which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1.0 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (including new capital property) above an exclusion threshold, and 20% on excess spending. Meanwhile, Ontario (retaining its $3.0 million cap for the 8% refundable OITC and 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC), Alberta (retaining its $4.0 million cap for the 8%/20% Innovation Employment Grant), Saskatchewan (implementing a custom increase of its refundable CCPC threshold from $1.0 million to $2.0 million while capping total annual credits at $1.0 million), and the Atlantic and Prairie provinces continue to enforce distinct statutory parameters.
1. Federal Statutory Architecture and Program Economics
1.1 Dual-Pillar Legislative Framework under the Income Tax Act

The Canadian federal SR&ED tax incentive program operates as a statutory entitlement rather than a discretionary or competitive grant: any taxpayer—whether a corporation, individual (sole proprietorship), partnership member, or trust beneficiary—that carries on business in Canada and performs qualifying SR&ED work in Canada is legally entitled to claim the incentives upon satisfying the statutory conditions and strict filing deadlines. There is no application intake window, lottery, or ministerial discretion to ration credits.

The legislative architecture rests on five interlocking components of the Income Tax Act (the Act) and the Income Tax Regulations (the Regulations). First, Subsection 248(1) of the Act serves as the definitional gatekeeper, establishing the exhaustive legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" (SR&ED). It bifurcates eligible activities into basic research (paragraph (a)), applied research (paragraph (b)), experimental development (paragraph (c)), and eight enumerated categories of directly supporting work (paragraph (d)), while strictly excluding seven commercial, routine, or non-scientific activities under paragraphs (e) through (k). Subsection 248(1) also defines critical expenditure terms, including "salary or wages", "specified employee", and "specified shareholder".

Second, Section 37 of the Act establishes a dedicated, non-expiring tax pool for allowable current and (for property acquired prior to 2014 or after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada under Subsection 37(1). Taxpayers may deduct any portion of a positive pool balance against business income in the current taxation year or carry the undeducted balance forward indefinitely to offset future business income.

Third, Section 127 of the Act governs the calculation of "qualified expenditures" under Subsection 127(9), the generation of the basic 15% ITC under Subsection 127(5) and Subsection 127(9), and the 20% enhanced ITC addition (creating the combined 35% enhanced rate) for CCPCs and ECPCs under Subsection 127(10.1). Section 127 also codifies the expenditure limit rules (Subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.6)), non-arm's length expenditure transfers (Subsection 127(13)), reductions for government/non-government assistance and contract payments (Subsection 127(19)), anti-avoidance intermediary rules (Subsection 127(24)), the 180-day unpaid expenditure rule (Subsection 127(26)), and the 20-year ITC recapture regime (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36)).

Fourth, Section 127.1 of the Act authorizes the cash refund of unused ITCs earned in the taxation year under Subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01), and deems any refunded ITC to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable under Subsection 127.1(3) so as to prevent double utilization via carryback or carryforward.

Fifth, Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (Sections 2900–2903) specifies the "directly related" and "incremental" overhead tests under the Traditional Method (Regulations 2900(2) and 2900(3)), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) formula, salary base exclusions, overall cap, and specified employee restrictions under the Proxy Method (Regulations 2900(4) to 2900(9)), the definition of Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) excluded from Shared-Use Equipment (Regulation 2900(11)), Prescribed Expenditures excluded from earning ITCs (Regulations 2901 and 2902), and Special-Purpose Buildings (Regulation 2903).

body.text: 1.2 Program Scale, Claim Disposition, and Fiscal Expenditure Trends (2021/22–2027)

Empirical program statistics published by the CRA and tax expenditure projections published by the Department of Finance Canada demonstrate sustained expansion in both claim volume and dollar value. Between CRA fiscal year 2021/22 and fiscal year 2025/26 (fiscal years running April 1 to March 31), the number of SR&ED claims filed annually rose by 18.8%, from 20,332 to 24,160, while total SR&ED ITCs claimed increased by 44.1%, from $3.4 billion to $4.9 billion. Over the same four-year window, the average ITC sought per claim increased from approximately $167,000 to $203,000. In fiscal year 2024/25, the CRA processed 22,738 claims (22,758 filed) from more than 19,000 distinct claimants and delivered $4.5 billion in allowed credits, representing an average allowed credit of $198,000 per claim. In fiscal year 2025/26, total ITCs allowed reached $4.6 billion out of the $4.9 billion claimed.
Note: The CRA notes that the 2022/23 disposition percentages are rounded and do not add to exactly 100%.

From an administrative risk standpoint, CRA workload selection filters resolve the vast majority of claims without audit adjustments: in 2025/26, 90.0% of processed claims were accepted as filed, 6.0% were accepted after financial or technical modifications, and 4.0% were denied. Moreover, 95.0% of claims accepted as filed during initial workload selection were processed within 60 days. Where a claim is accepted without audit, the CRA typically processes the return and issues a refund cheque or tax reduction within 60 to 120 days of receipt; if selected for a technical and financial review or audit, processing times generally extend to 180 days or longer.

Sectorally, software development dominates the Canadian SR&ED landscape, capturing 42.6% of all SR&ED credits allowed in 2025/26. Industry calculations applying the CRA's field-of-science shares to total allowed credits indicate that software development grew by approximately 66% over four years—rising from roughly $1.18 billion in 2021/22 to approximately $1.96 billion in 2025/26—compared to approximately 24% growth across all other scientific fields combined. Other tracked fields of science in the CRA statistics include materials engineering (4.6% of allowed credits in 2025/26, up from 4.5% in 2021/22), earth and environmental sciences (4.0%, up from 3.5%), agricultural sciences (2.2%, up from 1.9%), and food processing (1.3%, down from 1.5%).

By enterprise size (measured by gross income in 2025/26), small businesses (under $4 million in gross income) submitted 65% of processed claims and received 33% of allowed credits (in 2024/25, small businesses filed 64% of claims and received 32%, or $1.44 billion, of the $4.5 billion delivered). Small-to-medium enterprises ($4 million to $20 million in gross income) accounted for 20% of processed claims and 23% of allowed credits; medium enterprises ($20 million to $250 million) accounted for 12% of claims and 22% of allowed credits; and large enterprises (over $250 million) filed 3% of claims but captured 22% of allowed credits. Based on the Department of Finance Canada's Report on Federal Tax Expenditures 2026 (Part 2), industry tabulations put the combined federal fiscal cost of the SR&ED ITC at $4,941 million in calendar year 2024 ($2,205 million non-refundable), $5,176 million in calendar year 2025 ($1,970 million non-refundable), $5,331 million in calendar year 2026 ($2,035 million non-refundable), and $5,551 million in calendar year 2027 ($2,130 million non-refundable).
2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework (Subsection 248(1))
2.1 Statutory Definition of SR&ED

Under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of three core categories. The first category, basic research (Paragraph 248(1)(a)), comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, with results typically published in scientific journals. The second category, applied research (Paragraph 248(1)(b)), comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and most common category claimed by Canadian businesses, experimental development (Paragraph 248(1)(c)), comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.
2.2 Directly Supporting Work (Paragraph (d)) vs. Excluded Work (Paragraphs (e)–(k))

Where a taxpayer establishes the existence of core basic research, applied research, or experimental development under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) carried on in Canada, Paragraph 248(1)(d) expands the definition of SR&ED to include work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive categories of support work—namely (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, and (8) psychological research—provided that such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core (a), (b), or (c) work undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Support work is never SR&ED on its own. For example, computer programming appears on the Paragraph (d) list of support work; therefore, coding standard CRUD (create, read, update, delete) features, user dashboards, payment gateway integrations, routine debugging, or configuring cloud services by following vendor documentation does not qualify as SR&ED. Software development qualifies only when a genuine technological uncertainty exists—such as designing a novel algorithm or distributed system architecture when published methods and standard engineering fail to meet a strict latency, concurrency, or accuracy constraint—and the programming is commensurate with and directly in support of resolving that technological uncertainty.

Conversely, Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude seven categories of activity from the definition of SR&ED: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection.

As the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives (published August 13, 2021, and last updated July 5, 2022) emphasize, the decisive factor distinguishing eligible Paragraph (d) support work (such as "data collection" or "testing") from excluded Paragraphs (f) and (k) work ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") is purpose. If testing or data collection is conducted specifically to test a hypothesis aimed at resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty, it qualifies as Paragraph (d) support work; if it is conducted for commercial quality assurance, regulatory compliance, or general business operations, it is statutorily excluded. Similarly, if a mining or energy company performs eligible experimental development on a novel extraction process while simultaneously prospecting for minerals, the experimental development qualifies for SR&ED, but all work with respect to mineral prospecting must be carved out under Paragraph 248(1)(h).
2.3 Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance and the "Why" and "How" Requirements

CRA administrative guidance on what constitutes eligible SR&ED work has evolved through four historical phases, all anchored to Subsection 248(1) of the Act. Prior to 1985, Revenue Canada relied on Interpretation Bulletin IT-439, which the Department of Finance subsequently recognized as inadequate to explain the boundary between routine development and eligible R&D. On May 23, 1985, Finance Minister Michael H. Wilson tabled budget papers amending the regulatory definition to add the term "experimental development", clarifying that projects involving only routine engineering or routine development were excluded. On March 4, 1986, the Department of Finance confirmed three overarching criteria—(1) scientific or technological advancement, (2) scientific or technological uncertainty, and (3) systematic and organized investigation advancing the understanding of scientific or technological relationships—which Revenue Canada and industry leaders codified in Information Circular IC 86-4 (1986) and its 1994 revision IC 86-4R3 (alongside a December 2, 1992 legislative clarification confirming that experimental development includes incremental improvements undertaken to achieve technological advancement).

In 1998, Justice Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada issued the landmark ruling in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), synthesizing the concepts in IC 86-4R3 and Subsection 248(1) into a five-question judicial test. The CRA formally adopted Justice Bowman's five questions in its 2012 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (revised in 2015 and archived in August 2021):

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: In August 2021, following its 2020 modernization initiative, the CRA replaced the archived 2015 Policy with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives, which reorganize the five Northwest Hydraulic questions into two overarching statutory requirements: the "Why" requirement (corresponding to Questions 1 and 4) and the "How" requirement (corresponding to Questions 2, 3, and 5).

Under the "Why" requirement, work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement—meaning the generation or discovery of conceptual knowledge (theories, structural relationships, or prediction models) rather than mere factual measurements. New conceptual knowledge is needed only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists, which occurs when publicly available scientific/technological knowledge and internal business experience are insufficient to determine whether a given result or objective can be achieved or what alternatives (such as system architectures, equipment configurations, or circuit techniques) will achieve it. Indicators that available technological knowledge is insufficient include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, requirements or specifications conflict with existing standards, too many interlocking variables or unknowns exist, parameters or conditions lie outside normal operating ranges, or cost constraints force a departure from known engineering solutions. Crucially, acquiring existing knowledge or know-how through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve technological advancement. Conversely, commercial or technical failure does not disqualify a project: learning through systematic experimentation that an approach cannot work generates new technological knowledge and satisfies the "Why" requirement.

Under the "How" requirement, work must be carried out as a systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis. A systematic approach to work alone is not enough. The investigation must encompass four sequential steps: (1) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for resolving the uncertainty; (2) testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change as a result of testing; (3) developing logical conclusions based on the findings of the experiment or analysis; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

When framing a claim under CRA Guide T4088 (Guide to Form T661), an "SR&ED project" comprises a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary to resolve the scientific or technological uncertainties in the attempt to achieve the specific scientific or technological advancements defined for the project, pursued through a systematic investigation by qualified individuals. The CRA determines project eligibility at the level necessary to recognize all required work, including Paragraph (d) support work. The statutory completion date of an SR&ED project is defined as the point at which the claimant (1) achieved the scientific or technological advancement by resolving the associated uncertainties, (2) determined that the scientific or technological uncertainties cannot be resolved, or (3) terminated the project for any reason.
3. Federal SR&ED Tax Incentives: Rates, Thresholds, and Post-December 15, 2024 Reforms
3.1 Evolution from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Budget 2025 and Bill C-15

When auditing or preparing corporate SR&ED claims spanning the 2024–2026 period, tax practitioners must distinguish between the initial draft proposals in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) and the final statutory parameters enacted by Bill C-15 (which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026) following the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget.

Under legacy rules applicable to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) earned the enhanced 35% ITC on up to $3.0 million of annual qualified expenditures (yielding a maximum annual refundable federal credit of $1,050,000), phasing out when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (on an associated basis) was between $10 million and $50 million. While the December 2024 FES initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit to $4.5 million (which would have yielded a maximum $1,575,000 refundable credit), the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget further increased the annual expenditure limit from $4.5 million to $6.0 million, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. At the 35% enhanced rate, a qualifying CCPC or Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) can now earn up to $2.1 million annually in 100% refundable federal ITCs on current SR&ED expenditures. Simultaneously, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds were raised to $15 million and $75 million, eligibility for the 35% enhanced rate was extended to ECPCs, and capital expenditures (including leased equipment and Shared-Use Equipment) were restored for property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024.

body.text: 3.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas and Mathematical Mechanics
A. Qualifying Income Limit and Taxable Capital Reduction Formula (Subsections 127(10.2) & 127(10.21))

Under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), a corporation's expenditure limit is adjusted based on the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (or, where applicable, 3-year average annual gross revenue) across the associated corporate group. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit was reduced on a straight-line basis by $0.075 for every $1.00 of previous-year taxable capital employed in Canada between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, using the underlying qualifying income limit formula $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A is nil if taxable capital is $10,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the excess of taxable capital over $10,000,000.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the gradual reduction of the $6,000,000 maximum expenditure limit begins at $15,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada and reaches nil at $75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out band). As documented in the CRA's October 7, 2026 Policy, the underlying qualifying income limit formula is $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount of taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000. (While earlier September 2025 commentary based on the $4.5 million FES draft cited a reduction rate of $0.075 per $1.00 over the $60 million band, scaling the CRA's $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000] formula to the enacted $6,000,000 maximum expenditure limit reduces the $6,000,000 limit on a straight-line basis by $0.10 for every $1.00 of prior-year taxable capital or 3-year average gross revenue between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000.)
B. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the Revenue Method (Subsections 127(9), 127(10.32), 127(10.6))

To qualify as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) under Subsection 127(9) for a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative conditions throughout the taxation year: (1) be resident in Canada; (2) have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Canadian-resident corporations all or substantially all of the shares of which are owned by one or more ECPCs are also eligible for the enhanced refundable ITC.

Under Subsection 127(10.6), ECPCs calculate the straight-line phase-out of their $6,000,000 expenditure limit using their average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (fully eliminated at $75,000,000). Members of a corporate group that prepare consolidated financial statements must calculate gross revenue based on the highest level of consolidation presented to shareholders across all corporations that are members of the group in the taxation year for the 3 preceding fiscal years (regardless of whether the corporations were associated during the entirety of that 3-year period), and group members must share and allocate the single $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Non-group members use gross revenue from their GAAP financial statements presented to shareholders.

Crucially, under Subsection 127(10.32), a CCPC may elect on the prescribed form to determine its expenditure limit using the 3-year average annual gross revenue phase-out structure under Subsection 127(10.6) instead of the prior-year taxable capital structure. This election allows capital-intensive private companies (such as biotechnology, clean-tech, or hardware ventures that have raised over $15 million in equity or debt financing—inflating their taxable capital employed in Canada—while remaining pre-revenue or below $15 million in 3-year average gross revenue) to select whichever methodology yields the higher expenditure limit.
C. Short Taxation Years, Associated Corporations, and Venture Capital Relief Rules

Where a corporation has a short taxation year, or where a CCPC (or ECPC) has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated (or in the same consolidated group) in two or more of those tax years with another CCPC (or ECPC) having a tax year ending in that same calendar year, specific proration rules apply under Subsection 127(10.5). As illustrated in the CRA's Policy, if an associated group shares a $3,000,000 expenditure limit (or $6,000,000 post-December 15, 2024) and Corporation P has a 184-day taxation year running from July 1 to December 31, 2027, Corporation P's expenditure limit is prorated as $3,000,000 × [184 days ÷ 365 days] = $1,512,328.

Associated CCPCs must allocate the annual expenditure limit among themselves using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). If two otherwise unassociated corporations are associated with the same third corporation, the Act deems them to be associated with each other; the statutory exceptions to third-corporation association apply only for the Small Business Deduction and do not apply to the SR&ED expenditure limit. However, to ensure that venture-backed small businesses are not inadvertently penalized when the same syndicate of unconnected venture capital or angel investors invests in multiple startups, the Act provides deeming relief provisions. Two CCPCs are deemed not to be associated for purposes of calculating the expenditure limit and refundable ITC if the sole reason they would otherwise be associated is that two or more investors own shares in each corporation, provided that (1) there is at least one shareholder of one of the corporations who is not a shareholder of the other corporation, and (2) the existence of that non-overlapping shareholder is not for the purpose of satisfying these relieving provisions.

body.text: Under Subsection 127(5), a taxpayer first applies available ITCs to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. Under Subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC that is refunded to the claimant in the taxation year is deemed to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in that year, thereby reducing the balance of ITCs available for carryback or carryforward. Any remaining unused ITCs may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years and carried forward for up to 20 subsequent taxation years. Where a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control, the carryforward of unused ITCs earned before the acquisition of control and the carryback of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control are restricted under Section 127. Finally, no amount may be included in a claimant's ITC in respect of an SR&ED expenditure made in the course of earning income if any of the claimant's income from that business is exempt from Part I tax under Section 149.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Statutory Restrictions
4.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Subsections 37(8), 37(10) & Regulation 2900)

For each taxation year, a claimant must choose between two mutually exclusive calculation methodologies to account for SR&ED overhead and indirect support costs: the Proxy Method (elected by ticking Line 160 of Form T661) or the Traditional Method (selected by ticking Line 162 of Form T661, or applied automatically by default if no election is made). Under Subsection 37(10) of the Act, this choice is made on an annual basis when Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that taxation year once filed.

body.text: Because the Proxy Method substitutes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the Part 5 salary base (Regulation 2900(4); previously 60% in 2013 and 65% in 2012 and prior years), it yields a larger Investment Tax Credit whenever a claimant's provable, directly related, and incremental overhead is less than 55% of its qualified SR&ED salary base. Most software, artificial intelligence, and SME claimants elect the Proxy Method because they avoid the heavy compliance burden of tracking and proving itemized overhead, and because fixed facility rent, standard monthly internet/telephone plans, and general utilities fail the "incremental" test under the Traditional Method. However, while the PPA generates ITCs (and any ITC claimed on the PPA reduces the subsequent year's Section 37 pool under Paragraph 37(1)(e)), the PPA itself cannot be added to the Section 37(1) deductible pool (the actual overhead expenses it represents are instead deducted as ordinary business expenses), whereas actual overhead under the Traditional Method enters the non-expiring Section 37(1) pool.
4.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and Foreign Work (Subsection 37(9.1) & Regulation 2900)
A. Directly Engaged vs. Indirect Support Employees

Under Subsection 248(1) and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment. Eligible SR&ED remuneration includes gross salaries, wages, inducements/non-competition payments for employment services, and cash or non-cash taxable benefits (provided non-cash benefits represent a reasonable estimate of actual employer cost, exclude GST/HST or PST unless no input tax credit can be claimed, and are not also deducted as regular business expenses), as well as bonuses and remuneration based on profits for non-specified employees. Conversely, the employer's share of payroll benefits (CPP, EI, EHT, health/dental plans), retiring allowances, and extended vacation or sick leave are excluded from direct SR&ED salary or wages (though employer benefits and retiring allowances for hands-on SR&ED staff may qualify on Line 360 as overhead under the Traditional Method). Stock option benefits (for options granted or shares issued on or after November 17, 2005) and shareholder dividends are completely excluded from SR&ED claims.

To be claimed on Line 300 (regular employees) or Line 305 (specified employees), the employee must be directly engaged in SR&ED—performing hands-on work in basic research, applied research, experimental development, or Paragraph (d) support work (preparing equipment and materials for tests, running experiments, collecting experimental data, recording measurements, preparing computer programs, or performing engineering/mathematical analysis), or acting as a first-line supervisor who directs the technical course of ongoing SR&ED. Certain hands-on tasks performed by non-specialized employees (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a test run) also qualify if supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications. If an employee spends all or substantially all (90% or more) of their time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary qualifies. Time spent on non-technological management, sales, fundraising, or clerical/administrative services (accounting, payroll, legal, HR, shipping, inventory control) is excluded from directly engaged wages.
B. Specified Employee Statutory Ceilings and Proxy Base Restrictions

A "specified employee" is defined in Subsection 248(1) as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a "specified shareholder"—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer or of any corporation related to the employer (including non-arm's length relatives such as a spouse or sibling of a 10%+ shareholder).

Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory caps and exclusions. First, all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are completely excluded from SR&ED salary or wages (both in Canada on Line 305 and outside Canada on Line 309). Second, under Subsection 37(9.1) of the Act, the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed for a specified employee (Line 305) is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the employer's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the taxation year. Notice that Line 305 does not impose a 75% time cap. If a specified employee performs SR&ED across two or more associated corporations, the single 5 × YMPE limit cannot be duplicated and must be allocated among the associated corporations using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).

Third, under the Proxy Method, Regulation 2900(7) restricts the amount of a specified employee's salary that may be included in the Part 5 salary base (Line 816) to generate the 55% PPA to the lesser of: (1) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (including both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits under Sections 6 and 7, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year per Regulation 2900(9)); and (2) 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed in Tax Year ÷ 365) (with no proration for days in the year when the employee was not a specified employee). Under Regulation 2900(8), associated corporations employing the same specified employee must share a single 2.5 × YMPE ceiling. For example, in a taxation year ending in 2026 (where YMPE is $74,600), an owner-manager paid $200,000 for 100% SR&ED work claims the full $200,000 on Line 305 (below the $373,000 5 × YMPE cap), but includes only $150,000 in the Part 5 PPA salary base (since 75% of $200,000 = $150,000 bites before the $186,500 2.5 × YMPE cap). Conversely, an owner-manager paid $250,000 for 100% SR&ED work in 2026 has 75% of salary equal to $187,500, which is capped at $186,500 in Part 5.

body.text: C. Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(6))

Even after applying the Part 5 salary base exclusions (Regulation 2900(9)) and specified employee caps (Regulations 2900(7)–(8)), Regulation 2900(6) imposes an overall cap on the PPA (calculated in Part 5, Section B of Form T661). Under Regulation 2900(6), the PPA claimed on Line 820 / Line 502 cannot exceed the corporation's total business deductions for tax purposes minus specified statutory deductions—such as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), Section 37 SR&ED pool deductions, and building rental/use costs (Formula: A − B − C). In practice, this overall cap restricts the PPA only when a company's non-SR&ED operating expenses outside those specified deductions are less than $55 for every $100 of base SR&ED salary.
D. Unpaid Remuneration (180-Day Rule under Subsection 78(4)) and Foreign Work (Subsection 37(1.5))

Under Subsection 78(4) of the Act, any employee remuneration incurred in a taxation year that remains unpaid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. Unpaid wages must be reported on Line 315 of Form T661 and are excluded from the current year's Section 37 pool and ITC calculation. Once actually paid in a subsequent taxation year, they can be claimed on Line 310 in that later year (though under Regulation 2900(9), prior-year unpaid wages deemed paid under Subsection 78(4) are excluded from the PPA salary base).

While contract expenditures for work performed outside Canada are excluded from the Section 37(1) pool and ITCs (and may only be deducted against income under Subsection 37(2)), Subsection 37(1.5) allows a claimant to claim permissible salary or wages for SR&ED carried on outside Canada (reported on Line 307 for regular employees and Line 309 for specified employees) for both the Section 37(1) pool and ITCs. To qualify, the foreign SR&ED work must be: (1) directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (not a contractor); (2) performed by an employee who was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) related to a business of the claimant; and (4) an integral part of the SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant (and not taxed in another country). Permissible foreign wages (Line 307 + Line 309) are capped at 10% of the total salary or wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada (measured against Line 306 under the Proxy Method, or against Line 306 plus eligible "undertake, supervise, or support" salaries on Line 360 under the Traditional Method).
4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Regulation 2900(2)(a) & Recapture)

Under Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Act, Paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations, and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, a claimant (under either the Traditional or Proxy Method) may claim 100% of the laid-down cost (invoice price, customs and excise duties, transportation, storage, and, for internally manufactured inventory, direct materials, direct labour, and manufacturing overhead) of materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, provided they are used directly in SR&ED in Canada (with non-arm's length purchases restricted to the supplier's actual cost excluding any profit element).

To pass the CRA's "body of a thing" test, the raw materials, substances, or items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible thing on which the SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED. Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless during the SR&ED work (such as chemicals, seed, agar, growth media, fertilizers, pre-treated process water entering a chemical stream, or metal parts tested to destruction). Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials that are changed or incorporated into a prototype, custom product, or commercial asset during the prosecution of SR&ED. If materials transformed (or experimental animals/plants) are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the ITC earned on those materials is subject to ITC Recapture under Subsections 127(27) to 127(36), unless proceeds or fair market value are less than 10% of the total cost (de minimis scrap rule).

Conversely, items that do not compose the body of the thing under investigation are strictly excluded from Lines 320 and 325. Excluded items include laboratory glassware and supplies (petri dishes, test tubes, pipettes, beakers, flasks, vials), cleaning products, solvents, lubricants (such as engine oil), CDs/DVDs, software licences, and general utilities or energy (electricity, natural gas, propane, oil, or general/boiler water used to operate equipment or maintain ambient temperatures). Such items can only be claimed as overhead on Line 360 if the claimant uses the Traditional Method and proves they are directly related and incremental.

body.text: Under Subsection 127(9), an arm's length contract expenditure qualifies for the 80% ITC inclusion only if it is paid or payable to a "taxable supplier"—defined as (1) a person resident in Canada, (2) a Canadian partnership, or (3) a non-resident person or non-Canadian partnership that receives the payment in the course of carrying on a business through a permanent establishment in Canada. Even if a foreign contractor performs the SR&ED work physically inside Canada, if that foreign contractor lacks a Canadian permanent establishment, 100% of the contract expenditure must be deducted on Line 528 of Form T661 and earns 0% ITC. (Note also that while the Subsection 37(14) "look-through rule" required payers to reduce contract expenditures by the performer's non-current capital expenditures between 2014 and December 15, 2024, the CRA's updated Capital Expenditures Policy confirms that contract expenditures and third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024 generally will no longer be reduced by the performer's capital expenditures.)

Where a founder or shareholder invoices the operating company (OpCo) through a personal Holding Company (HoldCo), the payment is treated as a contract expenditure rather than salary or wages. If HoldCo deals at arm's length with OpCo, only 80% counts toward the ITC (with no 55% PPA uplift). If HoldCo does not deal at arm's length with OpCo (Line 345), the contract payment is excluded from OpCo's qualified expenditures under Paragraph 127(9)(f) and earns 0% ITC directly. While the NAL performer (HoldCo) can transfer its own qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount) to OpCo using Form T1146 under Subsection 127(13), a severe statutory trap arises if HoldCo performs Paragraph (d) support work only (because support work on its own does not meet the definition of SR&ED for the performer). Moreover, Subsection 127(24) blocks taxpayers from circumventing NAL contract exclusions by inserting an arm's length intermediary between the payer and a NAL performer.

Third-party payments (reported on Line 370 of Form T661 with a separate Form T1263 for each payment) are included at 80% for ITC purposes and may be made to six classes of entities (): Entity A (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1))—corporations resident in Canada (tax incentives earned in the year the SR&ED is performed); Entity B (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii))—approved associations; Entity C (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii))—approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or similar institutions (universities and affiliated colleges hold automatic approval; others require approval from the Income Tax Rulings Directorate); Entity D (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii))—non-profit SR&ED corporations resident in Canada and exempt from tax under Paragraph 149(1)(j); Entity E (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii))—approved granting councils (such as NSERC matching industrial research chairs) that fund B, C, or D entities; and Entity F (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii))—Paragraph 149(1)(j) tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations performing basic or applied pre-competitive research in Canada. Payments in kind (property or services) to a university or college are valued at fair market value provided there are no conditions requiring direct or indirect payments back to the claimant.
4.5 Overhead, Cloud Computing, Software Licences, and Prescribed Expenditures (Regulations 2900 & 2902)

When a claimant uses the Traditional Method, current overhead and other expenditures claimed on Line 360 must satisfy two cumulative statutory tests under Paragraph 2900(2)(c) (prosecution of SR&ED) or Subsection 2900(3) (provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED). First, under the directly related test, there must be a direct linkage—with no intervening step or intermediary—between the expenditure and the SR&ED work, the hands-on SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used to perform SR&ED. For example, employer-paid related benefits or retiring allowances for hands-on SR&ED engineers have a direct linkage and qualify on Line 360, whereas employer-paid benefits, retiring allowances, travel, or training for clerical/administrative staff supporting those engineers have an indirect linkage and are disallowed. Second, under the incremental test, the expenditure (or allocated portion thereof) would not have been incurred had the SR&ED prosecution not occurred. Fixed monthly expenses—such as base office rent, fixed monthly telephone/cellular or internet plans, snow removal, or corporate accounting/legal fees—fail the incremental test. Conversely, variable electricity metered to SR&ED equipment, long-distance telephone charges directly tied to SR&ED, technological training in Canada for active SR&ED projects, travel and lodging in Canada to perform SR&ED testing at a customer location, clinical study volunteer fees, health and safety expenses, and moving expenses to relocate SR&ED employees to a Canadian facility pass both tests. Expenses related to selecting and hiring SR&ED personnel (headhunter fees, job advertisements, interview travel, and immigration/work permit costs) are excluded from SR&ED overhead and are deductible only as regular business expenses.

For software and AI companies claiming cloud computing costs (e.g., AWS, Azure) or software tools, bookkeeping systems must strictly segregate "production infrastructure" accounts from "development/R&D infrastructure" accounts, as only dedicated R&D computing costs may qualify. Under the Proxy Method, general overhead and indirect computing costs are covered by the 55% PPA (and intangible software/cloud subscriptions cannot be claimed as physical "materials" on Lines 320/325). Under the Traditional Method, incremental usage-based cloud computing costs directly linked to running SR&ED experiments qualify on Line 360.

Even if an expenditure is directly related and incremental (and thus deductible in the Section 37(1) pool), Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations designates specific "prescribed expenditures" that must be subtracted on Line 530 (or Line 532 for used capital property) of Form T661 and earn 0% ITC. Under Paragraph 2902(a), prescribed current expenditures include: (1) fees paid for preparing SR&ED claims; (2) costs to attend conventions or conferences; (3) interest and financing expenses; and (4) expenditures for General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF)—defined as desks, chairs, filing cabinets, photocopiers, fax machines, standard telephones, and calculators (note: computers, hardware, and software are not GPOEF). Under Paragraph 2902(b), expenditures to acquire used depreciable property are prescribed expenditures excluded from earning ITCs (subtracted on Line 532). Under Paragraph 2902(c) and Subsection 37(4), expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED are barred from both Section 37 deductions and ITCs.
4.6 Post-December 15, 2024 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs

Following a nearly 11-year repeal period (January 1, 2014 to December 15, 2024), Bill C-15 restored SR&ED tax incentives for capital property, Shared-Use Equipment, and leased equipment effective after December 15, 2024.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 (and Paragraph 37(1)(b) of the Act) if the property is depreciable property (under Subsection 13(21)) owned by the claimant, is available for use (under Subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, is not land, a building, or a leasehold interest in a building (excluded under Paragraph 37(8)(d)), and at the time of acquisition the claimant intended that it would either: (1) be used all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or (2) have ASA (90% or more) of its value consumed to perform SR&ED in Canada. Both new and used ASA equipment are 100% deductible in the Section 37(1) pool via Line 390 (and must not be claimed on Schedule T2SCH8 for CCA). However, only new ASA equipment (or equipment refurbished by a vendor prior to purchase to a current state-of-the-art "new state", or the claimant's own post-purchase refurbishment costs) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (which is 40% refundable at the 35% enhanced rate for CCPCs/ECPCs); used equipment is subtracted on Line 532 under Regulation 2902(b) and earns 0% ITC.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), if new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 does not meet the ≥ 90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 (and Part 6C) under Subsection 127(9), provided it is not GPOEF, is not a Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11), and is actually used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada. SUE is depreciated on Schedule T2SCH8 (not deducted in the Section 37 pool), and generates qualified expenditures for ITC purposes in two stages:

items: First Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): If actual SR&ED usage exceeds 50% of operating time during the first period (beginning when acquired/available for use and ending at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 12 months after acquisition), 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies on Line 504.

Second Term SUE (Additional 25% of Capital Cost): Provided the equipment qualified as First Term SUE and actual SR&ED usage exceeds 50% of operating time during the second period (beginning when acquired and ending at the end of the first taxation year that ends at least 24 months after acquisition), a second 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (totalling 50% across both terms) qualifies on Line 504.

Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) Disqualification (Regulation 2900(11)): If, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended to use the property for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing/processing facility or line [Reg. 2900(11)(c)] and intended to use it over its expected useful life primarily for non-SR&ED commercial purposes [Reg. 2900(11)(d)], the property is a PDP and is barred from SUE (0% ITC), even if unexpected technical problems cause actual SR&ED usage in the first 12 or 24 months to exceed 50%.

body.text: Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada (excluding building rent under Subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii)) are claimed based on operating time in the taxation year: (1) if used 90% or more (ASA) for SR&ED, 100% is claimed on Line 350 under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods (Proxy excludes GPOEF); (2) if used primarily (> 50% to < 90%) for SR&ED, Proxy Method claimants claim 50% of the lease cost (excluding GPOEF) on Line 355 (and 0% if used ≤ 50%), whereas Traditional Method claimants enter $0 on Line 355 and claim the exact proportional percentage of SR&ED usage on Line 360 as overhead (if directly related and incremental).
4.7 Unpaid Amounts (Subsection 127(26)), Government Assistance (Subsection 127(19)), and Recapture (Subsections 127(27)–(36))

Under Subsection 127(26), current SR&ED expenditures (other than salary or wages) incurred in a taxation year that are not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year for ITC purposes and must be deducted on Line 520 of Form T661. (For an unpaid arm's length contract, 20% is deducted on Line 529 and the remaining 80% is deducted on Line 520, leaving 0% in the current year; when paid in a later year, 80% of the paid amount is added back in Part 4.) Crucially, unpaid expenditures must be identified on Form T661 within the original 18-month reporting deadline for the year incurred, or they can never be included in qualified expenditures when subsequently paid.

Under Subsections 37(1)(d), 127(9), and 127(19), both the Section 37(1) pool and qualified expenditures must be reduced on a project-by-project basis by any government assistance (grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, or provincial R&D tax credits—reported on Line 429 / Line 514 for provincial assistance and Line 431 for other government assistance), non-government assistance (paragraph 12(1)(x) inducements), or contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date. However, pursuant to Bill C-69 (enacted June 20, 2024, amending Subsection 127(9) retroactively to January 1, 2020 for loans made after December 31, 2019), excluded bona fide loans with reasonable repayment terms from public authorities are generally not considered government assistance and do not reduce SR&ED expenditures. Non-arm's length parties may allocate assistance using Form T1145, and subsequent repayments of assistance are added back to the Section 37 pool (Paragraph 37(1)(c)) and Part 4 of Form T661.

Under Subsections 127(27) to 127(36) and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant acquired property (materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment, or tangible property from an arm's length SR&ED contract, but never salaries, overhead, materials consumed, or intellectual property) in the current year or any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 to 20 years by Subsection 127(36)), earned an ITC on that property, and sells the property or converts it to commercial use, the claimant must add to its Part I tax payable the lesser of the original ITC earned or the original ITC rate multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (arm's length sale) or fair market value (FMV) at conversion/NAL transfer (using notional Undepreciated Capital Cost [UCC] under Schedule 8 CCA rules as an accepted estimate of FMV for converted equipment). Recapture is waived under the de minimis scrap rule if proceeds or FMV are less than 10% of the total cost of the property. Any recaptured ITC is added back to the claimant's Section 37(1) pool in the following year under Paragraph 37(1)(c.2).
4.8 Worked Comprehensive Calculation: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method (2026 Taxation Year)

To demonstrate the exact statutory mechanics of the post-December 15, 2024 rules, consider InnovateTech Inc., an Ontario-based qualifying CCPC with a December 31, 2026 fiscal year-end, prior-year taxable capital of $8,000,000 (qualifying for the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit), and one SR&ED project in Toronto. During 2026, InnovateTech incurs: (1) $300,000 in direct SR&ED wages for 4 non-specified engineers (Line 300); (2) $200,000 in regular salary (plus a $30,000 bonus, which is disallowed) for its 100% founder/CEO working 100% on hands-on SR&ED (Line 305); (3) $40,000 in materials consumed (Line 320); (4) $50,000 for an arm's length Ontario engineering contractor (Line 340); (5) $100,000 for new ASA (≥ 90%) laboratory testing equipment acquired in 2026 (Line 390); and (6) $120,000 in provable directly related and incremental overhead (Line 360 if Traditional Method is chosen).

5.1 Dual Administration by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Department of Finance Canada

In Canada's institutional division of labour, the Department of Finance Canada sets legislative policy and drafts amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, while the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers both the scientific/technical review (conducted by CRA Research and Technology Advisors [RTAs]) and the financial/tax review (conducted by CRA Financial Reviewers [FRs]) of all federal SR&ED claims. The CRA also administers all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits through the unified federal T2/T1 tax system, with the sole exceptions of Quebec (where Revenu Québec administers provincial tax credits and financial verification while relying on the CRA's scientific eligibility review) and Alberta (where the Province of Alberta independently administers the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant).

body.text: The CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy distinguishes three late-filing scenarios. First, if Form T661 is not filed by the reporting deadline (even if Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) was filed on time), Subsection 37(12) deems the expenditures never to have been SR&ED expenditures; the claimant cannot deduct them under Section 37, cannot add them to the Section 37 pool, and earns 0% ITC. Second, if Form T661 is filed on time, but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the reporting deadline, the allowable expenditures properly enter the Section 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (and can be deducted against business income in the current or subsequent tax years), but the claimant is barred from earning any ITC (0% ITC) on those expenditures. Third, once expenditures have been timely identified on Form T661 to enter the Section 37(1) pool, the subsequent deduction of amounts from that pool in a later taxation year is not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline.
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes (2025–2026 Landscape)

Every Canadian province (except Prince Edward Island) and the Yukon Territory (unlike the Northwest Territories and Nunavut) offers a statutory R&D tax credit that stacks on top of the federal SR&ED ITC. However, provincial tax credits (other than in Newfoundland and Labrador for provincial calculation purposes) constitute "government assistance" under Subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act and therefore reduce the federal Section 37 deductible pool (Line 429) and federal qualified expenditures (Line 514) for the taxation year, unless the taxpayer formally waives or renounces a non-refundable provincial credit within the statutory deadline.

A. Quebec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul (Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization)

In its 2025–2026 Budget, the Government of Quebec enacted a fundamental overhaul of its provincial innovation tax regime for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, codified in Sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Quebec Taxation Act. The CRIC consolidates and replaces up to eight legacy provincial innovation measures—specifically abolishing and replacing (1) the legacy R&D Wage Tax Credit (which previously offered 30% for small CCPCs scaling down to 14%–20% for larger firms past asset ceilings), (2) the University and Public Research Centre Tax Credit (previously 35%–45% on 80% of contract value), (3) the Pre-Competitive Private Partnership Research Tax Credit, (4) the Research Consortium Membership Fees and Dues Tax Credit, and legacy foreign expert tax holidays.

While CRIC harmonizes its definition of core R&D with the federal Subsection 248(1) definition (and relies on the CRA to perform the scientific review of R&D activities), CRIC broadens provincial eligibility to cover pre-commercialization activities performed in Quebec as a continuation of R&D—including product design, prototyping, technological validation, testing, regulatory approval studies, and specific pre-commercial quality control work.

Unlike the legacy Quebec R&D wage credit, CRIC eliminates corporate size and asset tiers for its initial bracket, providing every eligible corporation operating in Quebec (whether a CCPC, public company, or foreign-owned subsidiary, except corporations claiming as members of a partnership, which are ineligible for the 30% enhanced rate) with a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of net eligible expenditures above the exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN, and prorated for short taxation years), and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on all eligible expenditures exceeding $1,000,000. Before the credit is calculated, total eligible expenditures for the taxation year must be reduced by an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 (prorated for short taxation years) or the sum across all eligible R&D and pre-commercialization employees of the Quebec basic personal amount ($18,571 / $18,751) multiplied by the percentage of each employee's time devoted to eligible CRIC activities.

Eligible CRIC expenditures in Quebec include: (1) 100% of Quebec salaries and wages paid to employees working on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization; (2) 100% of new capital property (CAPEX) acquired and first available for use in Quebec almost exclusively in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities (excluding land, buildings, rights in buildings, and equipment acquired for leasing); and (3) 50% of subcontracted work paid to arm's length Quebec subcontractors, universities, College Centres for the Transfer of Technologies (CCTTs), public research centres, and research consortia (replacing the legacy 80% inclusion rule for university/public research with a uniform 50% inclusion rule). CRIC does not provide a proxy overhead uplift. The credit is claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR (2025-09) alongside Form RD-222 and reported on the Quebec CO-17 return under Code 112 (R&D portion) and Code 113 (pre-commercialization portion) within 12 months after the CO-17 filing due date. When stacked with the 35% federal SR&ED ITC, a Quebec CCPC recoups up to 60%–65% of eligible R&D wage costs.
B. Ontario: Three-Tiered System (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Ontario operates three corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sched. A, all administered by the CRA. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96) provides an 8% refundable tax credit (10% prior to June 1, 2016) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum $240,000 refund). Ontario has not adopted the federal $6.0 million cap, although capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 became eligible for both the OITC and the ORDTC automatically when Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, as confirmed in the October 29, 2026 Ontario Fall Economic Statement; the $3,000,000 limit phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year specified paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 & 39; Schedule T2SCH508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) with no expenditure cap on Ontario qualified expenditures reduced by OITC and OBRITC. Unused ORDTC carries back 3 years and forward 20 years, or may be formally waived under Subsection 43(1) within 6 months of year-end to avoid reducing federal qualified expenditures as government assistance. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97; Schedules 568 & 569) provides a 20% refundable tax credit on up to $20,000,000 of annual qualified current expenditures paid in money (maximum $4,000,000 annual refund) under an eligible contract with an Ontario university, community college, hospital research institute, or Ontario Centre of Excellence, provided the corporation is not connected (> 10% voting shares or > 10% share FMV, or non-arm's length) to the institute.
C. British Columbia and Alberta: Contrasting Western Models

Under Part 6 (Sections 97–103) of the British Columbia Income Tax Act (claimed on Form T666 within an absolute 18-month deadline), British Columbia expressly aligned with the post-December 15, 2024 federal SR&ED expansion. B.C. provides a 10% refundable tax credit to both CCPCs and ECPCs on up to $6,000,000 of qualified B.C. expenditures (maximum $600,000 refund, doubled from $300,000), adopted the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital phase-out, formally restored capital expenditures, and in B.C. Budget 2026 made the provincial SR&ED credit permanent (with a 10% non-refundable credit available on excess expenditures and for non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporations, carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years).

Conversely, Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the AT1 filing due date and administered independently by the Province of Alberta—provides an 8% refundable benefit on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years), plus an additional 12% benefit (for a combined 20% refundable rate) on incremental spending above that 2-year base, up to a $4,000,000 annual expenditure cap. The IEG phases out over $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and, per June 30, 2026 provincial guidance, did not adopt the federal $6.0 million cap or wholesale capital expenditure restoration.

Because administrative guidelines issued by the CRA are not binding on the courts, every SR&ED dispute is ultimately governed by the statutory language of the Income Tax Act as interpreted by the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).
