body.text: 7.1 Detailed Case Law Analysis and Audit Defence Implications
1. Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839, TCC) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393)

In Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman established the bedrock five-criteria analytical framework that governs every SR&ED audit and Tax Court appeal in Canada, subsequently endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393). First, there must be a technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures—defined by Justice Bowman as techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Second, the person claiming SR&ED must formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, following a five-stage process: (a) the observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) the formulation of a clear objective; (c) the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (d) the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses. Third, the procedure adopted must accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the process must be undertaken to result in a technological advancement—meaning an advancement in the general understanding available to persons knowledgeable in the field, rather than knowledge known only to the claimant. Crucially, Justice Bowman confirmed that the failure of a hypothesis does not invalidate the claim: "The fact that the initial objective is not achieved invalidates neither the hypothesis formed nor the methods used. On the contrary it is possible that the very failure reinforces the measure of the technological uncertainty". Fifth, a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results must be kept as the work progresses.
2. Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6)

In Joel Theatrical Rigging, the appellant (JTR) designed and installed theatrical rigging and claimed two SR&ED projects: (1) the 2008 "Fire Curtain Project" to control the rate of descent of an 800-pound theatrical fire curtain within 30 seconds without counterweights using a motor, hydraulic pump, hoses, and valves across eight shop-floor experiments; and (2) the 2009 "Manual Override Project" to disengage a horizontal stage curtain cable drum during a power failure without losing the motor limit switch's calibration. At trial, JTR called only its president (who had a Grade 12 education and 36 years of rigging experience) and the accountant at the tax consulting firm that prepared its T661 claims; no professional engineer (P.Eng.) or engineering designer testified.

Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed the appeals for both years and established two crucial audit lessons. First, technological uncertainty exists in the mind of a specialist who identifies and articulates it; because no specialist or professional engineer testified, JTR failed to prove that a competent mechanical engineer could not have solved the counterweight-free fire curtain descent using routine hydraulic engineering (and four prior patents introduced by the tax consultant were given little weight because he was not an expert witness and could not explain the search terms used to locate them). Second, JTR's "Experiment Summary Sheets" were prepared by its tax consulting firm after all eight experiments had been completed, and listed the "hypothesis" for Experiment 2 in the "next steps" section of Experiment 1—leaving Experiment 1 with no pre-formulated hypothesis. Justice Sommerfeldt held that a scientific hypothesis must be a provisional statement formulated prior to testing, and emphasized that failing to preserve original shop-floor notes, sketches, and records created during the experiments places a claimant in a precarious position.
3. National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72, aff'g 2020 TCC 47)

In National R&D Inc., a software development claimant whose SR&ED claim met Criterion 1 (technological uncertainty) but failed Criteria 2 through 5 at the Tax Court appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal, arguing that (1) the Northwest Hydraulic test is merely non-binding guidance rather than a mandatory requirement under Subsection 248(1), (2) the CRA's August 2021 Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work removed the requirement to follow the scientific method and software engineering should be judged by an "engineering method", and (3) the TCC erred in excluding the taxpayer's second expert witness report.

The Federal Court of Appeal unanimously dismissed the appeal. First, echoing Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88), the FCA held that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are mandatory legal prerequisites (not mere guidance) through which courts give definition, amplitude, and precision to Subsection 248(1), though they are applied flexibly to applied sciences in light of the taxpayer's business environment. Second, the FCA held that the CRA's 2021 Guidelines did not remove the scientific method requirement and, in any event, CRA administrative guidelines are not binding on the courts. Moreover, the taxpayer's attempt to rely on an academic article distinguishing the "engineering method" from the "scientific method"—which had not been adduced through expert testimony at trial—was rejected as "an impermissible attempt to establish, through the back door, a fact that should be a matter of evidence at trial". Third, applying White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co. (2015 SCC 23), the FCA upheld the disqualification of the proposed expert witness because the taxpayer's sole shareholder and president had written 65% of the expert's report, destroying independence and impartiality and rendering the report "an exercise in advocacy", and because the report improperly opined on the ultimate legal question of whether the work qualified as SR&ED.
4. Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108) vs. Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2026 FCA 175)

The interplay between Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108) and Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2026 FCA 175, released October 21, 2026) defines the contemporary boundary of evidentiary proof in SR&ED litigation. In Canafric Inc., a manufacturer of custom frozen pies for major food retailers (Costco, Loblaws, Mortimer) claimed SR&ED across its 2013–2016 taxation years for 7 disputed projects involving extending preservative-free shelf life to 21 days, reducing sodium and fat, increasing protein, and preserving crust integrity after freezing. During the audit, the CRA Research and Technology Advisor dismissively remarked, "A pie is a pie what is the big deal about it", and disallowed the claims as routine "trial and error" lacking formal documentation. Chief Justice Rossiter overturned the CRA and allowed all 7 projects. Citing paragraph 12 of National R&D Inc. (2022 FCA 72), Chief Justice Rossiter held that the Northwest Hydraulic five-part test must be applied generously and contextually to non-traditional industries; because Canafric systematically analyzed why failed recipe batches did not meet target criteria before modifying them, it followed the scientific method. Furthermore, Chief Justice Rossiter held that while documentary evidence is advantageous, it is not strictly mandatory, and credible oral testimony from the CEO (Mr. Pandya) successfully bridged gaps in the written documentation.

Conversely, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175 (decided October 21, 2026), the Federal Court of Appeal established an essential appellate guardrail across 13 disputed SR&ED projects: a credible witness alone does not displace the Minister's reassessment assumptions. Even when a taxpayer's witness testifies honestly and credibly, the substance of that testimony and the supporting evidentiary record must still affirmatively establish all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria (as endorsed in RIS-Christie and C.W. Agencies) for each project claimed.
8. Audit Readiness and Compliance Verification Checklist

To ensure full statutory compliance and audit defence resilience under CRA technical (RTA) and financial (FR) reviews in 2026 and beyond, claimants and tax auditors should execute the following ten verification procedures prior to submitting Form T661 (Rev. 26) and Schedule T2SCH31:

items: Contemporaneous Technical Evidence Mapping (Form T661 Lines 270–282): Capture dated hypotheses, experimental test plans, failed test logs, time-tracking records, and prototype records as the work progresses, ensuring hypotheses are recorded prior to experimentation rather than reconstructed retroactively by consultants (Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6).

Strict Adherence to Part 2 Word Limits and CRDC Coding: Verify that Line 207 contains the 5-digit Statistics Canada CRDC 2020 v2.0 research code (RDF#####), Line 242 does not exceed 350 words, Line 244 presents a chronological narrative of hypotheses, experiments/analyses, results, and logical conclusions within 700 words, and Line 246 articulates the conceptual technological advancement within 350 words. Maintain completed Part 2 narratives on file at the place of business for all claimed projects, even when filing only the top 20 by dollar value.

CCPC Expenditure Limit Optimization (Taxable Capital vs. 3-Year Gross Revenue Election): For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, check whether the associated group's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000. If so, model whether electing the 3-year average annual gross revenue method under Subsection 127(10.32) preserves a larger portion of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit.

Irrevocable Proxy vs. Traditional Method Modelling (Lines 160 vs. 162): Perform a break-even calculation comparing 55% of the Part 5 salary base (net of Regulation 2900(7) specified employee caps and Regulation 2900(6) overall cap) against provable, directly related, and incremental overhead on Line 360 before filing Form T661, recognizing that the election on Line 160 or Line 162 is irrevocable for the taxation year once filed under Subsection 37(10).

Specified Employee Compliance (Subsection 37(9.1) & Regulation 2900(7)): Identify every employee owning 10% or more of any class of shares or dealing at non-arm's length with the employer. Exclude all bonuses, profit-based pay, dividends, and stock options; apply the 5 × YMPE cap ($373,000 for 2026) on Line 305; apply the lesser of 75% total salary and 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500 for 2026) cap on Line 816; and file Form T1174 if the specified employee works across associated corporations.

180-Day Unpaid Amounts Audit (Subsections 78(4) & 127(26)): Audit payroll and accounts payable ledgers as of the 180th day following fiscal year-end. Report any unpaid wages on Line 315 and any unpaid non-wage current expenditures on Line 520 before the 18-month reporting deadline so they remain eligible for inclusion in a subsequent taxation year when paid.

Subcontractor & HoldCo Structuring (Lines 340, 345, 528, 529): Confirm that every arm's length contractor on Line 340 is a Canadian resident or has a Canadian permanent establishment ("taxable supplier" under Subsection 127(9), avoiding a 100% exclusion on Line 528). Avoid routing founder or insider R&D labour through a non-arm's length HoldCo unless a valid Form T1146 transfer of qualified expenditures under Subsection 127(13) is executed for an eligible SR&ED project.

Post-December 15, 2024 Capital Property, SUE, and Lease Tracking (Lines 262, 263, 350, 355, 390, 504, 532): Maintain operating-time logbooks for all depreciable property and leased equipment acquired after December 15, 2024. Separate new vs. used ASA (≥ 90%) capital property (subtracting used property on Line 532 under Regulation 2902(b)), verify that Shared-Use Equipment (> 50% to < 90% actual use) is not disqualified as Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) by original commercial commissioning intent under Regulation 2900(11), and ensure Line 390 assets are not double-depreciated on Schedule T2SCH8.

Multi-Provincial Credit Stacking and Waiver Strategy: Coordinate federal Schedule T2SCH31 with provincial filings—specifically Form RD-1029.8.CR for Quebec's 30%/20% CRIC regime (accounting for the $50,000+ exclusion threshold and 50% subcontracting rule), Form T666 for British Columbia's expanded $6.0 million refundable credit, AT1 Schedule 29 for Alberta's 8%/20% IEG, and Schedules 566/508/568/569 for Ontario's OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC (evaluating whether to waive the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC under Subsection 43(1) to prevent grinding down the 35% cash-refundable federal ITC).

Absolute 18-Month Reporting Deadline Control: Calendar the statutory reporting deadline (18 months after corporate fiscal year-end; 17.5 months for individuals) with internal lock-dates well in advance, ensuring both Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND) are filed before the Lyrtech statutory bar expires.
